categories.name: Protocols

tools.by: Created by Anthropic, now in the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation

tools.name: A2A Protocol
tools.by: Created by Google, now a Linux Foundation project
tools.what: The agent-to-agent standard: agents publish an Agent Card, discover each other and hand off tasks over JSON-RPC, whatever framework they're built on.

tools.what: Infrastructure for agent networks. Its Agent Gateway Protocol (AGP) is now called SLIM: a secure messaging layer that can carry A2A and MCP traffic.

_research_shape: papers: id (arXiv id), year, title, by, theme, why, std/phase optional. benchmarks: name, id (arXiv), year, what, link. experiments: id, status (todo/progress/done, same as progress.json), q, method, result + link when done, phase, std, based (arXiv ids of the papers it builds on).

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.why: Showed that asking a model to reason step by step makes it much better at multi-step problems. Every agent's "think" step starts here.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.why: Interleaves reasoning with tool calls in one loop (reason → act → observe). The pattern Awaken is built on.

papers.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
papers.why: A model learns on its own when to call an API and what to pass it: the research root of function calling.

papers.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
papers.why: The agent writes a short critique of its failed attempt and keeps it in memory for the next try, with no retraining.

papers.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
papers.why: One model drafts, critiques and rewrites its own output in a loop. The simplest form of the reviewer role.

papers.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.why: Showed that text an agent reads (a web page, an email) can hijack it. The core threat behind sandboxing and least privilege.

papers.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
papers.why: 25 agents live in a simulated town with memory, reflection and planning. The classic memory architecture for agents.

papers.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
papers.why: Explores several reasoning paths and backtracks from dead ends, instead of committing to one chain.

papers.title: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
papers.why: Fine-tunes a model to call the right API with the right arguments across thousands of real APIs, and retrieves docs to stay current.

papers.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
papers.why: A Minecraft agent that writes its own skills as code and stores them in a growing library it reuses later.

papers.title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
papers.why: Gives agents company roles (PM, architect, engineer) and standard operating procedures so their hand-offs stay structured.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.why: Agents solve tasks by talking to each other, with humans able to join the conversation at any point.

papers.title: The Rise and Potential of Large Language Model Based Agents: A Survey
papers.why: A map of the whole field: the brain, perception and action of an agent, single and multi-agent setups, and open problems.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.why: Treats the context window like RAM and moves memories in and out of storage, so agents can work past the context limit.

papers.title: Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents
papers.why: CodeAct: agents that act by writing Python instead of JSON tool calls succeed more often. The idea behind smolagents.

papers.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
papers.why: Shows that designing tools for the agent (the agent-computer interface) matters as much as the model.

papers.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
papers.why: A test bed of realistic agent tasks with injection attacks built in, used to measure which defenses actually hold.

papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
papers.why: Studies hundreds of multi-agent traces and sorts the failures into a taxonomy: bad specs, agents talking past each other, weak verification.

benchmarks.name: SWE-bench
benchmarks.what: Real GitHub issues from Python projects. The agent must write a patch that makes the project's tests pass.

benchmarks.name: GAIA
benchmarks.what: Questions that are easy for people but need browsing, files and several tool calls for an assistant to answer.

benchmarks.name: WebArena
benchmarks.what: Self-hosted copies of real websites (shop, forum, GitLab, maps) where agents complete everyday web tasks.

benchmarks.name: OSWorld
benchmarks.what: Agents use a real desktop computer (apps, files, the OS) through the screen, mouse and keyboard.

benchmarks.name: τ-bench
benchmarks.what: An agent helps a simulated customer under company policy, scored on whether the final database state is correct.

benchmarks.name: AgentBench
benchmarks.what: Eight environments (OS, database, games, web shopping) that compare models acting as agents.

experiments.q: Can one neuron learn XOR, and what is the smallest network that can?
experiments.method: Train a single sigmoid neuron and a 2-layer network with hand-written backprop on the four XOR inputs.
experiments.result: One neuron can't separate XOR. A 2-layer network learns it. See the live demo.

experiments.q: Does an explicit "reason" step beat plain function calling on our tasks?
experiments.method: Run Awaken with and without the ReAct thought step on the same 20 tasks; compare success rate, steps and tokens.

experiments.q: Do code actions beat JSON tool calls for our agent?
experiments.method: Give Awaken the same tools as JSON schemas and as Python functions it calls in code; compare success and recoveries.

experiments.q: Does a written self-critique fix failed runs?
experiments.method: Re-run failed Awaken tasks with a one-paragraph critique of the last attempt kept in memory; count tasks fixed per retry.

experiments.q: Which memory works best for long tasks: sliding window, summaries or a vector store?
experiments.method: Run the same long multi-step task with each memory type; measure what the agent recalls correctly and the token cost.

experiments.q: Does a team of agents beat one agent with the same token budget?
experiments.method: Planner/Researcher/Executor/Reviewer vs one agent on the same tasks; tag each failure with the MAST taxonomy.

experiments.q: Can text the agent reads hijack our MCP tools?
experiments.method: Plant injection attempts in pages and files our agent reads; measure attack success with and without least-privilege tool permissions.

categories.name: Autonomous task agents
categories.blurb: Take an open goal, write their own task list and loop until it's done. The pattern that started the agent wave.

categories.name: Coding agents
categories.blurb: Work inside a codebase: read it, edit files, run tests and open pull requests.

categories.name: Computer-use & browser agents
categories.blurb: See a screen and drive the mouse and keyboard, so they can use websites and apps built for people.

categories.name: Research agents
categories.blurb: Search and read many sources over several minutes, then write a report with citations.

categories.name: Enterprise & customer-service agents
categories.blurb: Act on company systems (CRM, orders, tickets) under business rules, and hand off to a person when needed.

categories.name: Multi-agent workflows
categories.blurb: Several specialised agents wired into a graph, with a supervisor or fixed hand-offs between them.

items.name: AutoGPT
items.what: One of the first agents to take a goal, write its own task list and work through it with web search, files and memory. Today it's a platform for building and running agents.
items.system: One autonomous agent in a plan → act → observe loop

items.name: BabyAGI
items.what: A short Python script that creates, prioritises and executes tasks in a loop. It made the task-list agent easy to read and copy.

items.name: Manus
items.what: A general-purpose agent that runs research, coding and data-analysis jobs end to end in its own cloud computer.
items.system: General agent working in a cloud sandbox
items.note: Meta agreed to acquire Manus in December 2025.

items.name: Devin
items.what: Launched as an "AI software engineer": takes a ticket, plans, writes and tests code in its own shell, editor and browser, then opens a pull request.
items.system: Autonomous agent with its own dev environment
items.note: Cognition acquired the Windsurf IDE in July 2025.

items.name: Claude Code
items.what: An agentic coding tool for the terminal: reads the codebase, edits files and runs commands, asking permission before risky steps.
items.system: One agent with tools, human approval on risky actions

items.name: GitHub Copilot coding agent
items.what: Assign it an issue and it works in the background in a GitHub Actions environment, then opens a draft pull request for you to review.

items.name: Replit Agent
items.what: Builds and deploys an app from a prompt. Users see each step, like package installs and new files, and can step in.

items.name: Operator
items.what: Used its own browser to click, type and scroll through websites: filling forms, ordering groceries, booking appointments.
items.system: Computer-using agent: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
items.note: Folded into ChatGPT agent in July 2025; the standalone Operator closed in August 2025.

items.name: Claude computer use
items.what: A tool in the Claude API that lets the model read screenshots and control the mouse and keyboard of a computer you provide.

items.name: Project Mariner
items.what: A research prototype that browses and completes tasks in Chrome on your behalf.

items.name: Deep Research
items.what: Plans a search, reads and compares hundreds of sources over several minutes, and writes a cited report.

items.name: Gemini Deep Research
items.what: Turns a question into a research plan you can edit, browses the web for you, then writes a report with sources.
items.system: Research agent with a human-checked plan

items.name: Agentforce
items.what: Agents for service, sales and marketing that act on CRM data within guardrails, and escalate to a person when they should.

items.name: Sierra
items.what: Conversational agents that handle customer service for brands. The same team published the τ-bench benchmark.

items.name: Klarna AI assistant
items.what: Customer-support assistant for Klarna's shoppers. LangChain names Klarna as a LangGraph user and reports faster resolution times.

items.name: LinkedIn Hiring Assistant
items.what: A recruiter agent that sources, matches and messages candidates, so recruiters can focus on decisions.

items.name: Elastic Security agents
items.what: A network of agents for real-time threat detection in Elastic's security product.

items.name: Uber developer-platform agents
items.what: Agents that help run large code migrations and generate unit tests across Uber's codebase.
